Get Stoopy · Shop Smart. Live Better.Phase-1 review package · 2026-11-01
PROPOSED · NOT IMPLEMENTED

Architecture review,
before the first line of application code.

A centralized, secure, AI-enabled multi-vendor marketplace design for Bangladesh-first launch. This package consolidates the recovered conversation, master instructions and six visual references into reviewable architecture, data, permission, API, security and delivery decisions.

Review gate: approve or revise the proposed architecture before Phase 2. No paid resources, live payments, identity-document collection or production deployment are authorized by this document.

Honest status

The workspace originally contained references only. This is a Phase-1 design package, not a running marketplace. Document validation and diagram rendering are not application, security or payment tests. Phase 1 remains pending owner review; Phases 2–11 have not started.

Proposed core

  • Next.js BFF + one NestJS modular monolith + worker.
  • PostgreSQL/PostGIS, Prisma, scoped repositories + RLS.
  • Keycloak identity with opaque revocable sessions; mandatory privileged TOTP.
  • Immutable balanced finance journals; COD custody separate from earnings.
  • Recipient-first remote ordering; manual vendor ready; atomic 30-second rider offers.

Critical risks

  • Marketplace fund custody / QR / payout authority is not established by a gateway logo.
  • Cross-scope leakage must be tested in APIs, reports, exports, caches, sockets and AI.
  • Money/assignment races require DB constraints, not frontend or Redis-only locks.
  • KYC/session compromise and insider exports need strict access, step-up and audit.
  • Browser capture prevention and background GPS have real platform limits.

Source coverage: 802 normalized master/Bengali lines, 39 historical additions, 75 screenshot inventory rows. The original master attachment was not independently archived; byte-for-byte fidelity is not claimed. Unavailable historical artifacts are disclosed.

Decisions to approve

  1. Topology: Next.js BFF + NestJS modular monolith + worker, one business database.
  2. Identity: Keycloak operating cost vs maintained database-session auth alternative.
  3. Geography: separate Mymensingh City and Purbadhala pilot scopes; destination-based order visibility; explicit financial-scope anchor.
  4. Delivery/finance: store→recipient road-distance slabs, acceptance-time snapshot, Sunday cutoff/holiday policy, COD offset disclosure, commission precedence and vendor settlement hold.
  5. Providers: capability-gated adapters; QR/split settlement/disbursement disabled until contract/legal verification.
  6. Privacy/AI: consented first-party data, scoped read tools, human exact-action approval; no autonomous sensitive execution.
  7. Brand/client: approved red/white/black layout, mobile-first PWA, honest native/browser limitations.

Architecture approval permits development with labelled test fixtures only. It does not approve paid services, real money or production.

BN-310-001masterআচ্ছা স্ক্রিনশটে এর ফিচারগুলা এড করা নেই, এই জিনিসটারে তুমি এড করে দিবে যে যে ফিচারগুলো উল্লেখ করা আছে, একটা ইনফরমেশনও যেন মিছ আউট না হয় তাহলে কিন্তু অনেক বড় লস হয়ে যাবে, তুমি প্রত্যেকটা ইনফরমেশন রিট করে এবং তোমাকে আমার চ্যাট ডিভিডির কনভারসেশনও দিয়েছি সেগুলো ফলো করবে এবং স্ক্রিপ্টটা দিয়েছি সেটাও ফলো করবে ইনফরমেশনও যেন মিস না যায়। আর সিকিউরিটির বিষয়টা তো সব সময় মাথায় রাখতে হবে তোমার আর কন্টাকনোলজি দিয়ে করবে সেটাও বলা আছে।All phasesSource instruction

DESIGN DOCUMENT · 00-master-instructions.md

GET STOOPY

ENTERPRISE MULTI-VENDOR E-COMMERCE MARKETPLACE

MASTER AGENTIC DEVELOPMENT INSTRUCTIONS

Brand Name: Get Stoopy
Tagline: Shop Smart. Live Better
Business Model: Multi-Vendor E-Commerce Marketplace
Initial Market: Bangladesh
Expansion Markets: United States → Worldwide
Project Type: Enterprise-Grade, Secure, AI-Enabled, Multi-Country Marketplace

1. YOUR ROLE AS AN AUTONOMOUS DEVELOPMENT AGENT

Act as a complete senior software engineering team consisting of:

  • Principal Software Architect
  • Senior Frontend Developer
  • Senior Backend Developer
  • Database Architect
  • UI/UX Designer
  • DevOps Engineer
  • Cybersecurity Engineer
  • Payment Integration Engineer
  • AI/ML Engineer
  • QA Automation Engineer
  • Performance Optimization Engineer

Your responsibility is to plan, architect, develop, test, document, and prepare the complete Get Stoopy marketplace for production.

Do not create a simple demo website.

Build a scalable, maintainable, secure, production-oriented enterprise application.

Work independently through clearly defined development phases.

Do not skip architecture, security, testing, database design, or documentation.

Do not claim that a feature is complete unless it has been implemented and tested.

2. BRAND IDENTITY AND DESIGN SYSTEM

Use the approved Get Stoopy homepage design as the primary visual reference.

Brand identity:

  • Primary: Premium Get Stoopy Red
  • Secondary: Black / Deep Charcoal
  • Background: White
  • Supporting: Light Gray
  • Highlight: Subtle Champagne Gold where appropriate

Design rules:

  • Maintain the approved homepage layout.
  • Use red only for the existing red brand accents, buttons, promotional highlights, active states, and selected icons.
  • Keep ordinary backgrounds white.
  • Keep navigation and footer dark where shown in the approved design.
  • Do not replace the approved brand identity with a green theme.
  • Use consistent typography, spacing, shadows, borders, and button styles.
  • Make all pages responsive for mobile, tablet, laptop, and desktop.
  • Use accessible colors and keyboard navigation.
  • Avoid excessive animations, unnecessary gradients, and heavy visual effects.

Brand tagline:

"Shop Smart. Live Better."

Create a reusable design system with centralized theme tokens.

3. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE

Build one centralized marketplace backend and database.

Do not create separate databases for Customer, Vendor, Rider, or Admin.

Use separate role-based portals connected to the same authorized backend.

Required portals:

  1. Customer Website
  2. Customer Account Dashboard
  3. Vendor Dashboard
  4. Rider Dashboard
  5. Local Admin Dashboard
  6. City Admin Dashboard
  7. Regional Admin Dashboard
  8. Country Admin Dashboard
  9. Super Admin Dashboard

Architecture requirements:

  • Modular monolith initially.
  • API-first design.
  • Event-driven background processing where appropriate.
  • Clearly separated business modules.
  • Shared authentication and authorization services.
  • Centralized audit logging.
  • Country-specific configurations.
  • Future microservice extraction should remain possible.

Do not introduce unnecessary microservices during the first development stage.

4. RECOMMENDED TECHNOLOGY STACK

Use the following stack unless a documented technical reason justifies a better alternative.

Frontend:

  • Next.js
  • React
  • TypeScript
  • Tailwind CSS
  • shadcn/ui

Backend:

  • Node.js
  • NestJS or a well-structured Next.js backend architecture
  • REST API with documented OpenAPI specifications

Database:

  • PostgreSQL
  • Prisma ORM
  • PostGIS for geographic operations

Realtime:

  • Redis
  • Socket.IO

Background Processing:

  • BullMQ

Authentication:

  • Secure session-based authentication
  • Auth.js or a suitable established identity provider

Storage:

  • Private cloud object storage
  • Encrypted document storage

Maps:

  • Google Maps Platform or a suitable mapping provider

Testing:

  • Vitest or Jest
  • Playwright
  • API integration tests
  • Security testing

Infrastructure:

  • Docker
  • CI/CD
  • Managed PostgreSQL
  • Cloud monitoring
  • WAF
  • Encrypted backups

Pin dependency versions and maintain a dependency lockfile.

5. GEOGRAPHICAL HIERARCHY

Create a configurable geographic hierarchy:

Global → Country → Division / Region → District → City / Upazila → Service Zone → Neighborhood

Super Admin can create and manage all geographical areas.

Each Admin receives an assigned geographic scope.

An Admin must never access data outside their assigned scope.

Enforce geographic permissions on the backend and database query layer.

Example:

A Mymensingh City Admin cannot access Dhaka City financial records.

A Zone Admin cannot manage another Zone.

Super Admin has global access.

Use PostGIS polygon-based service-area validation.

6. CUSTOMER WEBSITE

Create the complete Get Stoopy shopping experience.

Required pages:

  • Homepage
  • Product Listing
  • Product Details
  • Category Pages
  • Search Results
  • Deals and Offers
  • Wishlist
  • Shopping Cart
  • Checkout
  • Order Tracking
  • Customer Account
  • Order History
  • Return and Refund Requests
  • Customer Support
  • Privacy Policy
  • Terms and Conditions

Homepage sections:

  1. Brand Header
  2. Search Bar
  3. Navigation Menu
  4. Hero Banner
  5. Shop by Category
  6. Promotional Banners
  7. Trending Products
  8. Recommended Products
  9. Featured Vendors
  10. Best Sellers
  11. New Arrivals
  12. Trust and Security Section
  13. Newsletter
  14. Footer

Product cards must support:

  • Product image
  • Product title
  • Current price
  • Original price
  • Discount
  • Rating
  • Wishlist
  • Add to Cart
  • Stock availability

All product information must come from the database.

Do not hardcode production product listings.

7. CUSTOMER AUTHENTICATION

Create Login, Registration, Password Recovery, and Email Verification.

Supported authentication:

  • Email and Password
  • Google
  • Facebook
  • LinkedIn
  • X/Twitter

Use secure OAuth/OIDC integrations where supported.

Requirements:

  • Email verification
  • Password hashing using Argon2id
  • Secure session management
  • Refresh-token rotation where applicable
  • Account linking protection
  • Login rate limiting
  • Suspicious-login detection
  • Password recovery
  • Optional customer MFA

Never store plaintext passwords.

Social sign-in must be configured using legitimate provider credentials and approved OAuth applications.

8. KYC VERIFICATION SYSTEM

Create a dedicated KYC module.

Vendor KYC:

  • National ID
  • Profile photograph
  • Trade License
  • Store information
  • Business information
  • Verified bank or MFS account

Rider KYC:

  • National ID
  • Profile photograph
  • Address
  • Emergency contact
  • Driving License when applicable
  • Vehicle information when applicable

Admin KYC:

  • Identity verification
  • Super Admin approval
  • Secure administrative account provisioning

KYC statuses:

  • Pending
  • Under Review
  • Verified
  • Rejected
  • More Information Required
  • Expired

Support self-service document upload and authorized office-assisted document upload.

Use encrypted private storage, restricted access, short-lived signed URLs, reviewer audit logs, and retention policies.

Use only authorized identity-verification services and lawful verification channels.

Do not scrape government identity databases.

A Vendor cannot sell until approved.

A Rider cannot accept deliveries until approved.

9. GOOGLE AUTHENTICATOR AND ADMIN SECURITY

Make Google Authenticator-compatible TOTP mandatory for:

  • Super Admin
  • Country Admin
  • Regional Admin
  • City Admin
  • Zone Admin
  • Other privileged administrative accounts

Authentication flow:

  1. Email and Password
  2. TOTP Verification
  3. Session Risk Evaluation
  4. Dashboard Access

First-time setup:

  • Generate TOTP secret securely.
  • Display enrollment QR code.
  • Verify initial six-digit code.
  • Generate recovery codes.
  • Store secrets encrypted.

Additional protections:

  • Email challenge for new or suspicious devices.
  • Session expiration.
  • Device management.
  • Session revocation.
  • Login history.
  • Security notifications.
  • Step-up authentication for sensitive actions.

Admin accounts must be created or invited by authorized administrators.

No public Admin registration.

Never allow an AI agent to bypass authentication or authorization.

10. CUSTOMER LOCATION AND REMOTE ORDERING

Provide two checkout options:

  1. Deliver to Myself
  2. Deliver to Someone Else

The Buyer and Recipient must be separate entities.

A Buyer in Dhaka must be able to order a product for a Recipient in Mymensingh if that destination is supported.

The Recipient's delivery address determines:

  • Available Vendors
  • Service Zone
  • Delivery Fee
  • Rider Eligibility
  • Delivery ETA

Buyer GPS must not be required to match Recipient location.

Use buyer IP, device, GPS, and VPN indicators only as risk signals where lawful and appropriate.

Do not claim VPN detection is perfect.

Use phone verification, risk scoring, and additional verification when needed.

Initially disable cross-border ordering, but design the architecture to support future expansion.

11. MULTI-VENDOR ORDER MANAGEMENT

Support multiple vendors in a single customer checkout.

Create:

  • One Parent Order
  • Separate Vendor Suborders

Each Vendor can see only their own suborder.

Order workflow:

Customer Order → Vendor Pending → Vendor Accept / Reject → Preparation Time Set → Ready for Pickup → Rider Assignment → Pickup → In Transit → Delivered → Completed

Vendor must manually confirm Ready for Pickup.

Do not automatically mark orders ready when preparation time expires.

If a Vendor rejects an order, execute the configured refund or cancellation workflow.

Support partial cancellation and partial refund where applicable.

Use database transactions and idempotency to prevent duplicate orders and financial operations.

12. RIDER DASHBOARD

Create a mobile-first Rider Dashboard.

Features:

  • Rider Profile
  • KYC Status
  • Start Shift
  • End Shift
  • Online / Offline Status
  • GPS Location
  • Delivery Offers
  • Order Acceptance
  • Pickup Navigation
  • Customer Navigation
  • Pickup Confirmation
  • Delivery Confirmation
  • Recipient OTP
  • Delivery History
  • Earnings
  • COD Ledger
  • Wallet
  • Payout History
  • Support

GPS tracking should operate only during an active shift or active delivery, subject to clear consent and privacy controls.

Use zone-based rider eligibility.

13. SMART RIDER DISPATCH

When Vendor confirms Ready for Pickup:

  1. Find eligible online Riders in the correct service zone.
  2. Calculate road-route distance from Rider to Vendor.
  3. Sort eligible Riders by the configured dispatch priority.
  4. Offer the delivery to the nearest eligible Rider.
  5. Give the Rider 30 seconds to accept.
  6. If rejected or timed out, offer it to the next eligible Rider.
  7. Continue until accepted or escalation is required.

Use atomic assignment and database locking to prevent two Riders from receiving the same final assignment.

Do not rely only on straight-line GPS distance when road-route distance is required.

Use Redis and realtime events where appropriate.

14. RIDER DISTANCE-BASED EARNINGS

Create an Admin-controlled fixed-distance payment system.

Do not calculate extra Rider earnings from traffic, waiting time, or unrelated time spent outside delivery work.

Super Admin must configure:

  • Distance slabs
  • Rider payment per slab
  • Minimum delivery payment
  • Optional maximum payment
  • Country
  • City
  • Service Zone
  • Effective date
  • Active / Inactive status

Example configuration only:

0–2 km = configurable amount

2–4 km = configurable amount

4–6 km = configurable amount

These are examples, not final business rates.

Calculate eligible delivery distance using the configured routing method.

Snapshot the applicable rate when the delivery is assigned or otherwise according to the approved pricing policy.

Do not silently change historical earnings when Admin updates future rates.

Only successful completed deliveries generate normal Rider earnings.

15. RIDER WALLET AND SUNDAY PAYOUT

Create a dedicated Rider Earnings Ledger.

Each successful delivery creates an earnings credit.

Maintain separate balances for:

  • Delivery Earnings
  • COD Cash Collected
  • COD Amount Due to Company
  • Verified COD Deposits
  • Approved Deductions
  • Pending Payout
  • Paid Payout
  • Withdrawable Balance

Default payout schedule:

Every Sunday.

Support:

  1. Automatic Payout
  2. Manual Withdrawal Request

Automatic payout should be the default enabled option, subject to a verified and supported payout destination.

Provide a separate bank-account withdrawal option.

Do not assume a Rider can receive a bank payout without providing verified bank details.

If a Rider has COD outstanding, show the adjustment transparently.

The Rider must be able to see a complete transaction history and the calculation of their withdrawable amount.

Use immutable financial ledger entries.

Do not reset a balance to zero by deleting or overwriting transactions.

16. COD MANAGEMENT

Support:

  • Cash collected from Customer
  • Cash deposited at Company Office
  • Bank Deposit
  • Approved Merchant MFS Deposit

Admin verifies deposits.

Maintain a complete COD reconciliation history.

Do not automatically consider an unverified deposit as paid.

17. PAYMENT GATEWAY

Bangladesh payment integration must support a provider adapter architecture.

Evaluate:

  • SSLCOMMERZ
  • amarPay
  • shurjoPay

Do not assume all providers support marketplace split settlement or centralized dynamic Bangla QR.

Verify actual provider contracts, APIs, merchant eligibility, and regulatory requirements before implementing the collection and settlement flow.

Payment options:

  • Online Payment
  • Bangla QR, if supported by the selected acquiring provider
  • Cash on Delivery

Payment requirements:

  • Server-side verification
  • Signed webhook verification
  • Idempotency
  • Payment reconciliation
  • Refunds
  • Chargebacks
  • Failed-payment handling
  • Transaction history

Never treat a screenshot as proof of payment.

For international expansion, use suitable country-specific payment providers.

Do not hardcode Stripe or any other provider as universally available.

18. VENDOR COMMISSION AND SETTLEMENT

Create configurable marketplace commission rules.

Commission can be configured by:

  • Country
  • City
  • Zone
  • Vendor
  • Product Category
  • Order Type

Support percentage-based and fixed commission rules.

Calculate commission according to the configured successful-order policy.

Default commission basis should be product subtotal, excluding delivery fee unless explicitly configured otherwise.

Vendor Dashboard must display:

  • Gross Sales
  • Marketplace Commission
  • Refunds
  • Adjustments
  • Net Payable
  • Pending Settlement
  • Completed Settlement
  • Settlement History

Vendor settlement must use verified payout destinations and authorized approval workflows.

19. AI PERSONALIZATION ENGINE

Create a privacy-respecting product recommendation engine.

Use permitted first-party marketplace signals:

  • Product Searches
  • Product Views
  • Wishlist
  • Cart Activity
  • Purchase History
  • Product Comparisons
  • Category Preferences
  • Explicit User Preferences

Show:

  • Recommended for You
  • Frequently Viewed Products
  • Similar Products
  • Frequently Bought Together
  • Recently Viewed
  • Trending in Your Area
  • Personalized Deals

Use consent-based preference storage.

Allow customers to view, manage, and clear personalization data.

Do not secretly listen to phone calls or record WhatsApp, IMO, Viber, Facebook, or other applications.

Do not attempt to access private communications or microphone data from other apps.

If voice-based product search is offered, it must be an explicit user-initiated feature with microphone permission.

Use first-party website activity and authorized data sources only.

20. FRAUD DETECTION ENGINE

Create a configurable fraud-risk engine.

Risk signals may include:

  • Repeated COD refusals
  • Duplicate order patterns
  • Suspicious order velocity
  • Coupon abuse
  • Duplicate payment indicators
  • Repeated OTP failures
  • Unusual account behavior
  • Device and network risk indicators

Risk actions:

  • Allow
  • Require Verification
  • Hold for Manual Review
  • Reject Confirmed Fraud

Suspicious orders should be held for review rather than automatically rejected solely because of VPN usage or IP location.

Maintain:

  • Risk Score
  • Risk Reasons
  • Evidence
  • Reviewer
  • Decision
  • Audit History

Use rate limiting and CAPTCHA or equivalent bot protection where appropriate.

21. SUPER ADMIN DASHBOARD

Create a premium, fully responsive Super Admin Dashboard.

Modules:

  • Global Overview
  • Country Management
  • Region Management
  • City Management
  • Zone Management
  • Admin Management
  • Vendor Management
  • Rider Management
  • Customer Management
  • Orders
  • Products
  • Categories
  • Commission Rules
  • Rider Rate Configuration
  • Rider Payouts
  • Vendor Settlements
  • COD Reconciliation
  • Payment Management
  • KYC Review
  • Fraud Management
  • AI Configuration
  • Marketing
  • Coupons
  • Notifications
  • Reports
  • Audit Logs
  • Security Settings
  • System Health

Super Admin can manage the complete platform.

Sensitive financial, access-control, and KYC actions require appropriate authorization and audit records.

22. LOCAL ADMIN DASHBOARD

Create a geographically restricted Admin Dashboard.

Features:

  • Regional Overview
  • Local Orders
  • Customers
  • Vendors
  • Riders
  • Product Monitoring
  • Complaints
  • Returns
  • Local Delivery Operations
  • Local Reports
  • Local Analytics

An Admin cannot change their own geographic scope.

Only an authorized higher-level Admin can modify assignments.

23. VENDOR DASHBOARD

Features:

  • Store Overview
  • Product Management
  • Inventory
  • Product Variants
  • Orders
  • Accept / Reject
  • Preparation Time
  • Ready for Pickup
  • Sales Analytics
  • Commission
  • Earnings
  • Settlement
  • Customer Reviews
  • Return Requests
  • Store Profile
  • KYC
  • Support

A Vendor must only access their own business records.

24. CUSTOMER DASHBOARD

Features:

  • My Profile
  • Saved Addresses
  • Wishlist
  • Cart
  • My Orders
  • Remote Orders
  • Order Tracking
  • Returns
  • Refunds
  • Notifications
  • Recently Viewed
  • Personalized Recommendations
  • Support
  • Privacy and Personalization Controls

25. ADMIN DATA SECURITY

Implement defense in depth.

Requirements:

  • Server-side RBAC
  • Geographic ABAC
  • MFA
  • Session Revocation
  • Secure Cookies
  • CSRF Protection
  • CSP
  • TLS
  • Rate Limiting
  • Input Validation
  • SQL Injection Protection
  • XSS Protection
  • Secure File Upload
  • Encryption at Rest
  • Encryption in Transit
  • Audit Logs
  • WAF
  • Dependency Scanning
  • Security Monitoring
  • Encrypted Backups

Admin screenshot protection:

  • Use Android FLAG_SECURE in supported native Android applications.
  • Detect supported screen-capture events on iOS and mask sensitive content where possible.
  • Use dynamic visible watermarks in web dashboards.
  • Restrict clipboard and bulk export where practical.
  • Never claim that a browser can universally prevent screenshots or external-camera capture.

Create an Emergency Security Lock that authorized Super Admins can use to revoke active privileged sessions and trigger alerts.

Do not expose sensitive database credentials or secret keys to frontend code.

26. AI ADMIN ASSISTANT

Create an AI assistant with role-based permissions.

It may:

  • Summarize reports
  • Analyze sales
  • Recommend inventory actions
  • Detect unusual patterns
  • Draft product descriptions
  • Answer routine operational questions

It must not independently execute sensitive operations such as:

  • Money transfers
  • Vendor payouts
  • Rider payouts
  • Refund approvals
  • Admin permission changes
  • KYC approvals
  • Financial ledger modifications

Require authorized human approval for sensitive actions.

Log AI tool usage and decisions.

27. INTERNATIONAL EXPANSION

Start with Bangladesh.

Prepare country-level configurations for:

  • USA
  • Future International Markets

Each country must support its own:

  • Currency
  • Payment Providers
  • Tax Rules
  • Languages
  • Admin Structure
  • Service Zones
  • KYC Policies
  • Delivery Rules
  • Settlement Rules
  • Legal Configuration

Use country-specific merchant and legal arrangements.

Do not enable international cross-border checkout until the relevant operational and legal requirements are satisfied.

28. DATABASE DESIGN

Design normalized database models for at least:

  • User
  • Role
  • Permission
  • Session
  • AdminScope
  • Country
  • Region
  • District
  • City
  • ServiceZone
  • Address
  • Vendor
  • VendorKYC
  • Rider
  • RiderKYC
  • Customer
  • Product
  • ProductVariant
  • Category
  • Inventory
  • Cart
  • CartItem
  • Order
  • VendorSuborder
  • OrderItem
  • Delivery
  • RiderAssignment
  • RiderLocation
  • Payment
  • Refund
  • CommissionRule
  • VendorLedger
  • RiderLedger
  • CODLedger
  • Payout
  • Settlement
  • KYCReview
  • FraudCase
  • Notification
  • ProductInteraction
  • AuditLog

Use foreign keys, indexes, constraints, transaction boundaries, and suitable data-retention rules.

Use immutable ledger entries for financial transactions.

Prepare an ERD before implementing the complete database.

29. PERFORMANCE AND RELIABILITY

The website must be designed for speed and reliability.

Requirements:

  • Server-side rendering where appropriate
  • Optimized images
  • Responsive image sizes
  • Lazy loading
  • Code splitting
  • Database indexing
  • Query optimization
  • Pagination
  • Caching
  • CDN
  • Background jobs
  • Error monitoring
  • Structured logging
  • Graceful error handling

Avoid unnecessary client-side JavaScript.

Do not load every product or every order at once.

Use pagination and efficient APIs.

Do not claim zero latency or zero bugs.

Define measurable performance budgets and test them.

31. AGENTIC EXECUTION RULES

Follow these rules throughout development:

  1. Inspect the existing repository before modifying it.
  2. Preserve existing working features.
  3. Never overwrite user data without approval.
  4. Never expose production secrets.
  5. Use environment variables for credentials.
  6. Generate migrations instead of manually changing production databases.
  7. Run tests after meaningful changes.
  8. Fix errors before moving to the next phase.
  9. Maintain a development progress document.
  10. Keep an architecture decision record.
  11. Document incomplete integrations.
  12. Do not fabricate successful payment transactions.
  13. Do not use mock data as real production data.
  14. Clearly label demo data.
  15. Never deploy to production without explicit authorization.
  16. Ask for approval before creating paid cloud resources, registering paid services, or enabling real payment collection.
  17. Do not disable security controls to make tests pass.
  18. Keep the application accessible and maintainable.
  19. Use feature flags for unfinished or country-specific features.
  20. Do not mark a phase complete until its acceptance tests pass.

If a required API credential or provider agreement is missing, create a secure integration interface and document what is needed. Do not invent credentials or pretend the integration is live.

DESIGN DOCUMENT · 01-architecture.md

Get Stoopy — system architecture

Version: 0.1 • Date: 2026-11-01 • Status: Phase-1 review draft; not implemented or production-approved.

1. Inspection and scope

The workspace contained five uploaded reference images and no Git repository, source code, database, environment file, deployment or lockfile. No existing user data or working application was overwritten. The public conversation was recovered from its public share page, including user audio transcriptions. Source coverage and unavailable historical artifacts are recorded in 09-source-review.md.

This document proposes a production-oriented system; it does not claim that a marketplace, payment connection or security control already works. Implementation begins only after architecture review. No cloud resource, paid subscription or live payment collection has been created.

2. Architecture decisions

Area Proposed decision Reason / boundary
Application One TypeScript monorepo; Next.js web/BFF + one NestJS modular monolith API-first, explicit domain services and guards; no per-role backend
Data One PostgreSQL marketplace database, Prisma migrations; PostGIS Shared consistent orders and financial records, not four role databases
Identity Keycloak as the established identity provider; server-side BFF sessions Permitted alternative to Auth.js; central password/OIDC/TOTP lifecycle instead of custom security code
Web Next.js App Router, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, shadcn/ui, Zod, React Hook Form Shared design system, SSR catalog, accessible role portals
Async Separate worker process running the same domain code; BullMQ + Redis Retries, timeout jobs, payout scheduling, notifications; not a new business microservice
Realtime Socket.IO gateway inside API deployment; Redis adapter and authenticated rooms Horizontal event fan-out; database remains authoritative
Files Private S3-compatible object storage, quarantine bucket, KMS envelope encryption KYC never uses public product CDN
Maps Provider adapter; Google Maps Routes/Matrix candidate Road distance, not a straight-line substitute; credentials and budget required
Payments Provider adapters, capability registry, verified callbacks and reconciliation No universal split-settlement, payout or Bangla QR assumption
AI Permission-scoped module inside monolith; async jobs Earlier microservice suggestion superseded by master §3/§30; extraction only after measured need
Delivery network Owned rider network first; manual dispatch fallback; future courier adapter Hybrid/third-party option retained, not falsely integrated
Rider client Mobile-first PWA; optional native wrapper later No claim of reliable background GPS or browser screenshot blocking
Deployment Containers; web, API, workers and identity independently scalable Environments isolated; production requires separate explicit approval

Identity alternative: why not default to Auth.js credentials?

The master allows an established identity provider. Auth.js documents that its Credentials provider does not persist data by default and leaves password, rate limiting and recovery logic to the application; its project also announces that it has become part of Better Auth. We therefore propose Keycloak rather than combining a credentials-only JWT with separately implemented revocation and TOTP. Keycloak supports Argon2-family password hashing and TOTP policies; the implementation must explicitly select/test Argon2id parameters and Google Authenticator interoperability rather than assume a default meets the requirement. 1 1

This adds an identity service to operate. It is a documented trade-off, not a claim of lower complexity. If the owner rejects it, the fallback is a maintained session-based auth framework with a tested credentials/database-session adapter; do not silently substitute JWT-only auth.

3. System context

Browser / PWA
  → HTTPS + WAF/CDN
  → Next.js web + same-origin BFF (opaque HttpOnly cookie)
  → NestJS API: authentication context → RBAC → ownership / geographic ABAC
  → domain application service → scoped repository → PostgreSQL + PostGIS

Identity browser redirects ↔ Keycloak OIDC (Authorization Code + PKCE)
API ↔ Redis (cache, rate limits, location freshness, Socket.IO adapter)
API → transactional outbox → BullMQ worker → domain services / provider adapters
API ↔ private object storage (short-lived authorized access)
API ↔ maps, payment, notification and authorized KYC providers
Worker → immutable ledger, reconciliation, payout and notification jobs
All layers → redacted structured logs / metrics / traces / audit sink

The BFF forwards the cookie to the API over the same site. The API resolves the opaque session, current user status, roles, scope version and assurance. Provider access/refresh tokens stay server-side, encrypted; the browser does not receive database credentials, provider secrets or privileged bearer tokens. A future mobile client uses Authorization Code + PKCE and an explicitly reviewed token policy.

Proposed repository layout (not created as application code yet)

apps/web/                 Next.js pages, BFF, role portal layouts
apps/api/                 NestJS HTTP API and Socket.IO gateway
apps/worker/              BullMQ processors, schedulers, reconciliation
packages/ui/              shadcn-based accessible brand components
packages/contracts/       Zod schemas, generated OpenAPI types, event schemas
packages/config/          Validated server-only configuration and country flags
packages/testing/         Fixtures explicitly marked TEST_ONLY, contract helpers
prisma/schema.prisma      Application models; relation names follow data dictionary
prisma/migrations/        Reviewed forward migrations + PostGIS/constraint SQL
docs/                     Architecture, ADRs, runbooks, acceptance evidence
infra/                    Docker, CI, deployment templates; no secrets
 tests/unit|integration|e2e|security|performance/

Identity provider schema is owned and migrated by Keycloak, not Prisma. Use a separate schema and DB principals in the same approved PostgreSQL environment, or an isolated identity database if required by the provider's supported deployment. Neither option creates separate Customer/Vendor/Rider/Admin databases. Application User links to issuer+subject; it never treats Keycloak's console roles as marketplace authorization.

4. Module boundaries

Module Owns Does not own
Identity & access Canonical user link, sessions, roles, scopes, invitations, step-up Vendor eligibility or financial truth
Geography & country Administrative hierarchy, polygon versions, serviceability, country policy Buyer physical-location requirement
Catalog & inventory Vendor products, variants, moderation, availability/reservations Client-provided prices or stock totals
Checkout & orders Quote, buyer/recipient, parent/suborders, state transitions Provider settlement or rider assignment races
Delivery Shifts, consented locations, offers, assignments, route/rate snapshots, OTP Cash liability as earnings
KYC Cases, documents, individual decisions, expiry, authorized verification Government database scraping
Finance Payments, refunds, commission, balanced journals, COD, payouts/settlements Frontend confirmation or mutable balances
Trust & support Fraud evidence, review decisions, returns, tickets, SOS Automatic rejection solely for VPN use
Personalization & AI Consented interests, recommendations, scoped assistants Other apps' audio or autonomous sensitive operations
Marketing & loyalty Campaigns, coupons, subscriptions, rewards/referrals Unverified advertising claims or hidden fees
Platform Outbox/inbox, idempotency, notifications, audit, flags, health Business permission bypass

Each write goes through one application command. Workers and AI tools call the same guarded service, never raw SQL shortcuts. Cross-module synchronous calls have explicit interfaces; eventual projections use versioned events. Extract a service only for measured scaling, isolation or organizational need.

5. Order and delivery design

  1. Authenticate buyer; select Deliver to Myself or Deliver to Someone Else.
  2. Snapshot recipient name/phone/address separately. Resolve the destination polygon on the server. Buyer GPS is optional risk evidence, not an availability filter.
  3. Group eligible items by vendor and pickup store. Reserve inventory with an expiry; compute price, promotion, tax, per-group delivery fee and ETA from authoritative data. A quote has a version, hash and expiry.
  4. Create payment/COD intent, fraud decision and idempotency record. For prepaid orders, vendor fulfillment starts after verified payment unless an explicitly approved alternate policy exists.
  5. In one transaction create one parent, vendor/store suborders, item snapshots, recipient snapshot, initial status events and outbox events. A vendor sees only its suborder and minimum recipient fulfillment data, never other vendors' items or margins.
  6. Vendor accepts/rejects, sets preparation estimate, then manually confirms ready. Timer expiry never confirms readiness. Delay updates are audited and do not add waiting-time earnings.
  7. Ready event starts dispatch. PostGIS shortlists eligible riders; road-route matrix orders candidates. Offer to exactly one rider for 30 seconds using server time. Timeout/reject advances the sequence; exhaustion escalates to authorized local dispatch staff.
  8. Acceptance locks delivery and rider rows, rechecks offer expiry, KYC, shift, zone, capacity and stale location; creates one active assignment and rate snapshot. Socket messages are hints, not assignment authority.
  9. Pickup confirmation → in transit → recipient OTP verification → delivered. COD collection must be accounted before delivery completion. A failed delivery has an explicit exception/return workflow, not normal earnings.
  10. Completion emits immutable earning and commission events subject to the successful-order policy. Refunds/returns use reversing entries. Parent status is derived from suborders; partial fulfillment/cancellation remains visible.

Initial release: one suborder has one active rider; rider capacity defaults to one. Batching/multi-pickup optimization is a later flag, not an excuse for double assignment. Manual assignment uses the same eligibility and rate policies, with reason and audit trail. Courier integration remains disabled until a real contract/API exists.

Important state distinctions

  • Payment: INITIATED → PENDING_VERIFICATION → PAID / FAILED / CANCELLED; later PARTIALLY_REFUNDED / REFUNDED / DISPUTED.
  • Suborder: PENDING_VENDOR → ACCEPTED → PREPARING → READY_FOR_PICKUP → FULFILLING → DELIVERED → COMPLETED; rejection/cancellation are explicit branches.
  • Delivery: QUEUED → OFFERED → ASSIGNED → PICKED_UP → IN_TRANSIT → DELIVERED → COMPLETED; failed/return exceptions retain history.
  • KYC, fraud, payout and refund statuses are separate. The screenshot labels “Delivered” and “Completed” are not interchangeable financial events.

6. Authorization and data isolation

Every request builds an immutable AccessContext: user, session assurance, active roles, permissions, vendor memberships, rider identity, scope assignments and authorization version. Require permission and resource ownership/scope. A URL role prefix, hidden menu or client filter grants nothing.

The repository requires a typed scope predicate. Core tenant/geographic tables receive PostgreSQL row-level security as defense in depth. Within a transaction use SET LOCAL for verified actor/scope context; never interpolate client headers into SQL. Pooling must not leak session context. Migrations use a separate owner; runtime has no superuser or BYPASSRLS privilege. Super Admin global access is an explicit audited policy, not a shared database login.

RLS alone cannot express every business join. Service guards, scoped queries, RLS, field projection and negative API tests all remain required. See 03-role-permission-matrix.md and 04-geographic-model.md.

7. Financial integrity

Use balanced double-entry journals in integer minor units. VendorLedger, RiderLedger, CODLedger are purpose-specific views, not separate mutable wallets. A journal's debit total equals its credit total per currency; append-only constraints prevent update/delete. A business-event unique key prevents duplicate earning, deposit verification, refund or payout posting. Corrections are linked reversals.

Rider pay uses a versioned store-to-recipient road-distance slab captured on final acceptance (proposed policy). Rider-to-store road distance controls dispatch ordering, not extra earnings. Rate edits create future versions. Traffic may improve ETA but does not alter fixed slab pay. COD collected is a liability; only verified deposits reduce it. Payout reserves funds before sending; unknown provider outcomes reconcile the original attempt rather than blindly retrying a new transfer. See 06-finance-and-delivery-policy.md.

8. Failure behavior and reliability

Failure Required behavior
Payment callback delayed/duplicated Order remains pending; verify provider transaction; deduplicate event; reconcile
Maps unavailable No fake road distance or silent slab estimate; retry/queue or authorized manual exception
Redis unavailable Reject/rate-limit sensitive operations as configured; no unpaid privilege escalation; DB idempotency remains
Worker crash/retry Outbox/inbox + unique domain keys; safe replay; no duplicate financial effects
Socket disconnect Reconnect and fetch authoritative state; offer expiry still enforced in DB
Rider GPS stale/out of zone Stop new offers, warn/escalate; do not auto-cancel an active delivery or suspend solely for GPS noise
Provider payout result unknown Mark PROCESSING_UNKNOWN, reserve remains, reconcile before any retry
AI unavailable Ordinary search/catalog/checkout continue; assistant shows unavailable state
Primary DB failure Controlled write unavailability; tested restore/failover runbook; never invent successful writes

Initial proposed service objectives (to approve and test, not achieved results): monthly availability 99.9%; marketplace RPO ≤15 minutes and RTO ≤4 hours; identity recovery included in drills. Financial journal restore requires reconciliation before reopening payouts. No zero-downtime, zero-latency or zero-bug promise.

9. Performance budgets

  • Public landing/product pages: SSR/streaming, responsive AVIF/WebP, explicit dimensions, priority only for hero; lazy-load below fold.
  • Mobile reference conditions: 4G, mid-tier Android; p75 LCP ≤2.5s, INP ≤200ms, CLS ≤0.1. Initial route JS ≤200KB compressed excluding images; record exceptions.
  • API p95 ≤300ms for cached catalog reads and ≤700ms for non-provider order commands at the agreed pilot load; external provider latency reported separately.
  • Cursor pagination default 20, max 100; no unbounded orders/products; maximum search/filter complexity; no N+1 queries.
  • Explain plans for top queries; indexes for tenant/status/time, order references, variant/store stock and geography. Load-test realistic pilot concurrency before choosing capacity.
  • Cache public catalog by country/zone/currency/locale; never shared-cache authenticated pages, KYC, recipient data or financial responses. Invalidate by versioned events.
  • Dashboard charts aggregate server-side with scope and time range. Reference-image numbers are not benchmark results.

10. Deployment and operations

Local Docker Compose will provide PostgreSQL/PostGIS, Redis, identity, object-storage emulator and mail capture, all test-only. CI pins actions/dependencies, typechecks, lint/tests, migration checks, API contract checks, accessibility and security scans. Staging uses separate credentials/buckets/databases and provider sandboxes; production deployment is a separate authorized gate.

Managed PostgreSQL with PITR/encrypted backups, private networking, KMS, WAF, CDN, object scanning, secret manager, OpenTelemetry-compatible traces and an error tracker are proposed resources. None has been provisioned. Cloud choice, residency, budget, domain, merchant entity and on-call ownership remain decisions. Structured logs exclude passwords, session tokens, TOTP, full NID/bank data, recipient OTP and raw location streams. Audit storage is restricted and tamper-evident.

11. Critical risks and review gates

  1. Money movement authority: ordinary merchant APIs do not establish legal marketplace collection/split settlement. Central Bangla QR remains disabled until acquirer contract and flow are confirmed.
  2. Cross-scope leakage: destination-based order visibility, buyer residence and vendor location differ; test remote orders, reports, exports, sockets and AI against the same scope policy.
  3. Double spending/assignment: ledger, payout, inventory and rider races require database constraints and concurrency tests, not Redis locks alone.
  4. Identity and KYC exposure: mandatory admin TOTP, protected linking, encrypted documents, strict reviewer access and a tested emergency lock.
  5. Provider and mobile limits: OAuth apps, MFS payouts, routing, QR, background GPS and screenshot controls need real capability verification.
  6. Scope inflation: historical feature requests are retained but feature-flagged; secure core order/finance paths precede optional AI/loyalty/native features.
  7. Unverified reference claims: “worldwide shipping”, “free shipping on all orders”, payment logos and sample US contact details are not launch configuration.

Approval of this architecture authorizes Phase 2 implementation in a development environment only. It does not authorize paid services, real identity-document collection or production deployment.

DESIGN DOCUMENT · 02-api-architecture.md

REST API, event and realtime architecture

Status: versioned contract proposal; no API server exists. Machine-readable draft: ../contracts/openapi.yaml (also JSON). OpenAPI validation checks a document, not endpoint behavior.

Contract rules

  • Base path /api/v1; JSON UTF-8; REST resource nouns and explicit command subresources for business transitions. No client-selected database table or arbitrary SQL filter.
  • Browser uses same-origin BFF/session cookie. CSRF token and Origin validation on cookie-authenticated mutations. Provider callbacks have a separate adapter verification contract, not the customer cookie.
  • Server derives actor, role, vendor membership, country and geographic scope. Request adminScopeId is a selection within existing grants, never an expansion. Ignore/reject unknown privileged fields.
  • Idempotency-Key required for checkout, order transitions, rider acceptance, pickup/delivery, financial commands, payout requests, uploads and other replay-sensitive writes. Key scope = actor + operation; identical replay returns original result, different payload returns 409. Financial dedupe persists with linked records, not only a short Redis TTL.
  • Optimistic version / If-Match for mutable inventory, rules, profile and order commands; database locks still enforce invariants.
  • Cursor pagination default 20/max 100; limit, opaque cursor, validated sort and filters; response items, nextCursor. No unlimited export through list endpoints.
  • Money: {amountMinor: integer, currency: ISO4217}; display formatting is presentation only. Distance integer meters; timestamps UTC RFC3339; country timezone supplied separately.
  • Stable errors: {code, message, requestId, details?, retryAfterSeconds?}. 401 unauthenticated, 403 no permission/scope, 404 hidden/nonexistent resource under approved disclosure policy, 409 state/version/idempotency conflict, 422 domain validation, 429 rate limited. Do not expose SQL, stack traces, KYC numbers or tokens.
  • OpenAPI lists permission/scope metadata and planned phases. Public endpoint does not imply all underlying records are public.

Representative resource map

Area Endpoints / command families Guard and scope
Session authorize/callback, logout, sessions/devices, verification, linking, step-up OIDC state/PKCE/nonce; provider issuer+subject; session/CSRF checks
Customer profile, address book, privacy/consents, wishlist, cart Own customer account; no buyer-city access to other accounts
Catalog categories, products, variants, availability, search Public only approved country/zone catalog; owner/moderator writes
Checkout recipient validation, quote, order creation, payment intent Recipient destination country/zone; server prices/inventory/risk
Customer orders list/detail, tracking, cancellation, return, support Buyer ownership; signed tracking minimized/expiring; support scope
Vendor onboarding/KYC, stores, products/stock, suborders, prep/ready Vendor membership + store; current vendor KYC; own suborders only
Rider onboarding/KYC, vehicle, shift, location, offers, accept/reject Own rider, active KYC/shift/consent, valid zone/capacity
Delivery assignment, pickup, transit, OTP issue/verify, failure Active assignment or authorized dispatch scope; separate recipient proof
Finance wallet/ledger, COD deposit, payout destinations/requests, vendor settlement Owner or explicit financial grant; maker–checker + step-up
Admin geography, admin invites/scopes, KYC, rates/commission, orders, finance, fraud, audit, reports/export Explicit permission ∩ assigned scope ∩ assurance; no self-scope grants
AI scoped assistant, reports, approvals Caller∩agent scope; allowlisted read tools; no prohibited execution
Platform notification preferences, capabilities/flags, health Public capability metadata contains no secrets; sensitive flags admin-only

Key command contracts

Checkout

POST /checkout/quotes takes cart version, recipient address/contact, delivery mode and optional buyer-location evidence with consent. Response contains per-vendor/store group availability, item snapshots, price breakdown, delivery/ETA, policy/quote versions, hash and expiry. A quote is not an order or stock guarantee after expiry.

POST /orders takes quote ID/hash, idempotency key, payment method and consent references. Revalidate destination, vendor eligibility, stock, quote expiry and fraud status. Return authoritative order references and next action. Never accept client total/commission/rider pay. Prepaid fulfillment waits for server-verified payment. A pending provider result is not a paid order.

Vendor fulfillment

POST /vendor/suborders/{id}/accept, /reject, /preparation-time, /ready require ownership, allowed current state and version. Ready is a manual command with actor/time; preparation countdown cannot invoke it. Reject/cancel triggers the parent partial-state/refund workflow, not deletion.

Dispatch

Eligible rider receives only authorized offer metadata. POST /rider/offers/{id}/accept uses database time, token/ownership/expiry and locks; 409 OFFER_EXPIRED or ALREADY_ASSIGNED cannot be repaired client-side. Socket/push events carry IDs/version, not secret assignment authority. GET /rider/offers reconciles missed events.

Recipient OTP issuance goes to the verified recipient contact through a rate-limited channel. The rider submits the code but cannot choose the destination phone or read the hash. Buyer access alone does not prove they are the recipient. Exceptions require separate approval, evidence and audit.

Finance

POST /rider/cod-deposits submits evidence; it does not post verified funds. An authorized finance command verifies trusted bank/merchant/office evidence and posts the balanced deposit once. POST /rider/payouts creates a request/reservation only after eligibility checks. Approved execution is a worker/provider operation, never an AI or frontend “success” toggle.

Ledger read responses show opening balance, immutable entries, reversals, pending/reserved/paid amounts, COD due and withdrawable calculation. No PATCH /ledger or generic “set balance” endpoint exists.

Event architecture

Transactional outbox records are committed with business changes. Workers use inbox receipts and domain idempotency; at-least-once delivery is expected, exactly-once business effects are enforced by constraints. Envelope:

{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "eventKey": "opaque-unique-id",
  "eventType": "delivery.completed",
  "occurredAt": "2026-11-01T00:00:00Z",
  "countryId": "opaque-country-id",
  "scopeRefs": ["opaque-zone-id"],
  "aggregateType": "Delivery",
  "aggregateId": "opaque-delivery-id",
  "aggregateVersion": 7,
  "correlationId": "request-id",
  "causationId": "previous-event-id",
  "data": {"status": "COMPLETED"}
}

The example is illustrative, not a production record. Do not put raw NID, OTP, credentials or full bank data in events. Consumers re-read through guarded services when needed. Events include order.created, payment.verified, vendor.suborder.ready, delivery.offer.expired, delivery.assigned, delivery.completed, cod.deposit.verified, payout.status.changed, kyc.status.changed, scope.revoked, inventory.changed.

Socket rooms: user:{id}, vendor-store:{id}, rider:{id}, delivery:{id}, admin-scope:{grantId}. Join authorization runs server-side on connect and sensitive subscription; revoke rooms when scope/session changes. Customer location views use assignment-specific expiring tokens. Clients fetch state after reconnect; stale events cannot regress state.

API security/performance gates

Contract lint; generated types; request/response validation; negative RBAC/ABAC tests; concurrent idempotency tests; webhook replay; OTP/TOTP/session tests; pagination/filter bounds; query-plan budgets; rate-limit tests; no sensitive cache keys. No OpenAPI “Try it out” request in this review package reaches a backend or provider. Production CORS is an explicit allowlist; no wildcard credentialed access. Public API versioning is additive; breaking changes require a new version/migration plan.

DESIGN DOCUMENT · 03-role-permission-matrix.md

Role, ownership and geographic permission matrix

Status: proposed deny-by-default policy. Machine-readable companion: ../contracts/role-permission-matrix.csv.

Decision order

  1. Validate session, account status, authorization version and required assurance.
  2. Require an explicit permission for the command/resource.
  3. Resolve the target row and its owner/destination scope on the server.
  4. Apply vendor membership OR rider ownership OR admin geographic scope as appropriate.
  5. Project only allowed fields; apply step-up, maker–checker and export policy.
  6. Execute through a scoped transaction; audit sensitive reads, writes and denied attempts.

Legend: G = explicit global Super Admin policy; C/R/T/Z/L = assigned country/region/city/zone/local scope; O = own customer account; V = own vendor/store membership; D = own assigned delivery; — = no access. Scope never widens a role permission. “Review” is not authority to approve one's own case or financial action.
